# 404 Memory Found

> 404 Memory Found is a nostalgia blog about the technology, games, websites and companies of the 90s and 2000s: what they cost, why they won or lost, and what happened to them.

Every article is written under a pen name by the site's editorial team, sourced from primary documents (company filings, court records, contemporary reporting, museum collections) listed at the end of each post, and dated. Full text of every article, in Markdown: https://404memoryfound.com/llms-full.txt

## Hub pages
- [All posts](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/): every article, newest first
- [About and editorial policy](https://404memoryfound.com/about.html)
- [RSS feed](https://404memoryfound.com/feed.xml)

## Business Blunders
- [Who Owns Sears Now, and How Many Stores Are Left?](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/who-owns-sears-now-stores-left.html): Sears is owned by Eddie Lampert's Transformco and it is still trading. The last count found five full-line stores left, down from about 3,500.
- [Who Owns Atari Now? The Brand That Refuses to Die](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/who-owns-atari-now.html): Atari is owned by Atari SA in Paris and run by Wade Rosen. The brand sold for $5 million in 1998 and booked about $65 million last year.
- [Is Toys R Us Still in Business? What Survived 2018](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/is-toys-r-us-still-in-business.html): Toys R Us closed all 735 US stores on June 29, 2018. The brand survived: WHP Global owns it, and 1,664 stores now trade in 35 countries.
- [Is Palm Still a Company? From Pilot to a $349 Phone](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/is-palm-still-a-company.html): Is Palm still a company? No. HP bought it for $1.2 billion in 2010, sold webOS to LG, and TCL has owned the dormant Palm brand since 2014.
- [Is Blockbuster Still Open? The Last Store in 2026](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/is-blockbuster-still-open-last-store.html): Is Blockbuster still open? Yes, but only one store, in Bend, Oregon. Who owns the brand in 2026, how 9,000 stores became one, and what it sells.
- [Does AOL Still Exist? What You Get for $10 a Month](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/does-aol-still-exist-today.html): Does AOL still exist? Yes. Italy's Bending Spoons bought it for about $1.5 billion in January 2026, and dial-up died on September 30, 2025.
- [How Compaq Lost the PC Business It Helped Invent](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/compaq-lost-pc-business-hp-merger.html): Compaq went from a pie-shop sketch in 1982 to the world's biggest PC maker, then sold itself to HP for $25 billion. Here is what broke first.
- [Why Iridium Failed: The $5 Billion Satellite Phone](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/iridium-satellite-phone-failure.html): Iridium put 66 satellites in orbit for about $5 billion, opened for business in 1998, and filed for bankruptcy nine months later. It sold for $25 million.
- [The Beanie Babies Bubble: How a $5 Toy Went Bust](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/beanie-babies-bubble-what-happened.html): Beanie Babies were a $5 toy people traded like stocks in 1998. How Ty Inc. built the bubble, why it burst in 1999, and what the bears are worth now.
- [What Happened to the Sega 32X: The Add-On That Broke Sega](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sega-32x-add-on.html): In November 1994, Sega asked you to bolt a second console on top of your Genesis. It sold 665,000 units, then died in eighteen months. Here is the story.
- [The First Banner Ad: How One Click on October 27, 1994 Built the Modern Web](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/first-banner-ad-hotwired-1994-history.html): On October 27, 1994, an AT&T banner ad ran on HotWired with a 44 percent click-through rate. Three decades later, every website you use is shaped by what happened that day.
- [What Happened to theGlobe.com: The Biggest IPO Pop in History](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-theglobe-com-dot-com-ipo.html): In 1998 two Cornell undergrads took theGlobe.com public and watched the stock pop 606 percent on day one. It remains the largest first-day gain in IPO history. Here's the full story of how it happened and why it collapsed.
- [What Happened to Excite, the Search Engine That Turned Down Google for $750,000](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-excite-search-engine-google.html): In 1999, Excite was worth $35 billion and had the chance to buy Google for $750,000. CEO George Bell said no. The full story is more complicated, and a lot more interesting, than the punchline suggests.
- [What Happened to the TurboGrafx-16, NEC's Forgotten 16-Bit Console](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-turbografx-16-nec-forgotten-console.html): It was the king of Japan, the third option in America, and the console that invented half the things we now take for granted. Then it disappeared.
- [What Happened to PointCast and the 1990s Push Technology Boom](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-pointcast-push-technology.html): In 1997, News Corporation offered $450 million for a company that delivered headlines through a screensaver. Two years later it sold for $7 million. The full story of push technology's rise and collapse.
- [How the Nintendo NES Saved Video Games After the 1983 Crash](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-nintendo-nes-saved-video-games-1983-crash.html): In 1985, American retailers had given up on video games. Then a Japanese toy company shipped a gray plastic box with a robot, called it an entertainment system, and resurrected an entire industry. This is the full story of how the NES pulled gaming back from the dead.
- [What Happened to Standalone GPS Devices: TomTom and the Smartphone Killer](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-standalone-gps-tomtom-garmin-magellan.html): In 2008, the world bought 42 million standalone GPS devices. By 2014, the category was effectively dead. The story of how a free Android feature, a Cold War satellite system, and an $11 billion map data war ended an entire consumer electronics market.
- [What Happened to Wine.com and the Internet Wine Wars](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-wine-com-internet-wine-wars.html): Three companies burned through more than $200M trying to sell wine online between 1995 and 2001. The smallest one ended up owning the Wine.com domain.
- [What Happened to Prodigy, the Online Service That Beat AOL to America](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-prodigy-online-service.html): Before AOL, before the web, two of the biggest companies in America spent over a billion dollars trying to teach the country how to go online. Prodigy got there first, then lost everything.
- [What Happened to the 3DO, the $700 Console That Bombed](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-3do-700-dollar-console.html): In 1993, a console hit shelves at $699.99 and promised to be the VHS of gaming. Instead, the 3DO became one of the most spectacular flops in video game history. Here is the full story.
- [What Happened to Microsoft Bob, the Friendly Interface That Failed](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-microsoft-bob-friendly-interface.html): In 1995, Microsoft tried to replace the desktop with a cartoon house full of talking pets. It sold around 58,000 copies and got pulled from shelves within a year. Here is what really happened.
- [What Happened to Kodak, the Company That Invented the Digital Camera Then Chose to Ignore It](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kodak-digital-camera-bankruptcy.html): Kodak controlled 90% of the American film market, employed over 145,000 people, and invented the digital camera in 1975. Then it spent three decades pretending digital photography wasn't coming.
- [What Happened to the Segway, the Invention That Was Supposed to Change the World](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-segway-personal-transporter.html): Investors predicted a billion dollars in first-year sales. The Segway sold roughly 140,000 units across its entire twenty-year lifetime.
- [What Happened to Tumblr, the Platform Yahoo Bought for a Billion and Sold for Pennies](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-tumblr-yahoo-billion-dollar-mistake.html): Yahoo paid $1.1 billion for Tumblr in 2013. Six years later, Verizon sold it to Automattic for $3 million. Here's the full story of how a culture platform got killed by the companies that owned it.
- [What Happened to Flickr, the Photo Site Yahoo Left to Die](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-flickr-yahoo-photo-sharing.html): Flickr once hosted nearly 2 billion photos and defined photo-sharing for a generation. Then Yahoo acquired it, removed the features that made it special, and left it to rot while Instagram ate its lunch.
- [What Happened to the Sega Game Gear, the Handheld That Deserved Better](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sega-game-gear-handheld.html): The Sega Game Gear had superior hardware, full color graphics, and backlit brilliance. So why did it lose to the Game Boy? Discover the tragic tale of ambitious hardware sabotaged by battery life and Sega's own chaos.
- [What Happened to SimCity and How EA Destroyed It](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-simcity-ea.html): From Will Wright’s revolutionary city builder to EA’s catastrophic always-online launch, the rise and fall of SimCity is a cautionary tale about corporate mismanagement.
- [What Happened to Commodore, the Company That Won and Lost](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-commodore-computers.html): Commodore sold more home computers than anyone in history. Then its own executives drove it into the ground. Here is how it all fell apart.
- [What Happened to Neopets, the Virtual World That Raised a Generation](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-neopets-virtual-world.html): From 150 million accounts and $160 million acquisitions to corporate neglect and a management buyout. The full story of how Neopets rose, fell, and tried to come back.
- [What Happened to the Atari Jaguar? The Console That Killed Atari](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-atari-jaguar-64-bit-console.html): Atari bet everything on a '64-bit' console with a phone keypad controller and 63 games. It sold fewer units than some accessories.
- [What Happened to WordPerfect? The Software Microsoft Had to Kill Twice](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-wordperfect-word-processor.html): WordPerfect once held 85% of the DOS word processor market and earned $700 million a year. Then Windows happened.
- [What Happened to Lycos, the Search Engine Worth $12 Billion?](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-lycos-search-engine.html): Lycos went from Carnegie Mellon research project to the most visited site on the internet. Then it was sold for $36 million.
- [What Happened to HD DVD? The Format War That Cost Toshiba Everything](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-hd-dvd-format-war.html): Toshiba bet everything on HD DVD and lost to Blu-ray in a brutal two-year format war. Here's the full story of how Sony, the PS3, and one studio's decision ended it all.
- [What Happened to Lotus 1-2-3? The Spreadsheet That Built the PC Industry](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-lotus-1-2-3-spreadsheet.html): Lotus 1-2-3 was the original killer app, the reason businesses bought PCs. Then Microsoft Excel came along, and Lotus made one catastrophic strategic mistake.
- [What Happened to Netbooks? The $200 Laptops That Terrified Microsoft](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-netbooks-laptops.html): In 2007, ASUS released a tiny $299 laptop that launched a revolution. By 2009, netbooks were 10% of all PCs sold. By 2013, the category was completely dead.
- [What Happened to Gateway? The Cow Box Computer Company](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-gateway-2000-cow-box-computer.html): Gateway 2000 started on a cattle ranch in Iowa with a $10,000 loan and turned cow-spotted boxes into the most recognizable brand in personal computing. Then it all fell apart.
- [What Happened to Boo.com? The $135M Fashion Dot-Com Flop](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-boo-com-fashion-dot-com.html): Boo.com raised $135 million to sell designer fashion online, launched in 18 countries at once, and collapsed in six months. The concept was right. The timing was catastrophically wrong.
- [Motorola Razr V3: 130 Million Sold, No Signal Left](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/motorola-razr-v3-coolest-phone-ever-made.html): The Motorola Razr V3 sold 130 million units, and since August 3, 2026 it cannot make a call in the US. What one costs on eBay now.
- [What Happened to the Nokia N-Gage? The Gaming Phone That Became a Punchline](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-nokia-ngage-gaming-phone.html): Nokia spent hundreds of millions trying to merge phones and gaming consoles into one device. The result was a $299 taco-shaped punchline that sold 3 million units instead of the projected 6 million, got outsold 100-to-1 by the Game Boy Advance, and accidentally predicted the future of mobile gaming.
- [What Happened to Excite@Home? The $35 Billion Broadband Bet](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-excite-at-home-broadband.html): In 1999, Excite@Home had a $35 billion market cap, 4.1 million broadband subscribers, and a vision for the high-speed internet future. By 2001, the stock had crashed from $128 to $1, the company filed for bankruptcy, and millions of Americans nearly lost their internet access overnight.
- [What Happened to the Sega Saturn? The Console That Self-Destructed at Launch](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sega-saturn-console.html): Sega surprise-launched the Saturn at E3 1995 for $399, alienated every major retailer, and watched Sony destroy them with a single word: $299. The full story of gaming's most spectacular self-own.
- [Why the Apple Newton Failed and What It Costs Now](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-apple-newton.html): Apple sold about 50,000 Newton MessagePads in three months, then killed the line in 1998. Why it failed, and what a MessagePad sells for now.
- [What Happened to the Original Xbox? Microsoft's $4 Billion Bet on Gaming](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-original-xbox-microsoft-gaming.html): Four engineers, a gutted Dell laptop, and a plan to trick Bill Gates into building a gaming console. The original Xbox was never supposed to exist.
- [The AOL-Time Warner Merger: The Worst Deal in Corporate History](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/aol-time-warner-merger-worst-deal-in-history.html): In January 2000, AOL bought Time Warner for $182 billion. Within three years, the combined company posted the largest annual loss ever recorded. Here is how it fell apart.
- [What Happened to Kozmo.com? The Delivery App That Existed Before Your Phone Did](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kozmo-com-delivery.html): Kozmo.com raised $280 million promising free one-hour delivery of DVDs and snacks in 1998. It collapsed in 2001. Twenty years later, DoorDash proved the founders were right all along.
- [What Happened to Circuit City? The Store That Fired Its Way to Death](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-circuit-city-electronics.html): Circuit City was once the biggest electronics retailer in America. Then it fired 3,400 of its best employees, and everything fell apart.
- [How Amazon Survived the Dot-Com Crash (When Thousands Didn't)](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-amazon-survived-dot-com-crash.html): Amazon's stock fell 94% during the dot-com bust. The company was months from running out of cash. Here is why it survived when nearly everyone else didn't.
- [What Happened to Webvan? The Grocery Startup That Burned $800M](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-webvan-grocery-delivery.html): Webvan promised to revolutionize grocery shopping with 30-minute delivery windows and massive automated warehouses. Instead, it became the poster child for dot-com excess, burning through $800 million before collapsing in 2001. But was the idea really wrong, or just impossibly early?
- [Why the Nintendo GameCube Lost the Console War (But Won Our Hearts)](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-nintendo-gamecube-lost-console-war.html): Nintendo's little purple lunchbox sold just 21.74 million units against the PS2's 155 million. Here's how the GameCube got everything right except the stuff that mattered.
- [How eBay Went from a Broken Laser Pointer to a $30 Billion Empire](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/ebay-broken-laser-pointer-to-global-marketplace.html): In 1995, Pierre Omidyar sold a broken laser pointer for $14.83. By 1998, his side project had an IPO that tripled on day one. The full story of how eBay rewrote the rules of online commerce.
- [What Happened to RadioShack? The Store on Every Corner](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-radioshack-electronics.html): RadioShack had over 7,000 stores and helped launch the personal computer revolution. Then it forgot what made it special and destroyed itself from the inside.
- [What Happened to Friendster? The Social Network That Had It First](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-friendster-social-network.html): Friendster turned down $30 million from Google, attracted 115 million users, and proved people wanted social networking. Then it deleted everything and vanished.
- [What Happened to Fry's Electronics? The Store That Died Overnight](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-frys-electronics.html): Fry's Electronics went from themed megastores and $2.4 billion in revenue to closing every location overnight in 2021. Here's the full story of Silicon Valley's favorite tech store.
- [Is Encarta Still Available? Why Microsoft Killed It](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-microsoft-encarta.html): Microsoft Encarta is gone: disc sales ended in June 2009 and MSN Encarta closed October 31, 2009. What replaced it, and how to run it now.
- [The Rise and Fall of MySpace: How It Lost to Facebook](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/rise-and-fall-of-myspace.html): MySpace was the king of social media before Facebook took over. Learn how MySpace rose to 100M users, what went wrong, and why it collapsed so fast.
- [Why Google Glass Actually Failed: The $895 Million Experiment That Made You Look Like a Creep](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-google-glass-actually-failed.html): Google Glass was supposed to be the future of computing strapped to your face. Instead it became the fastest way to get banned from a bar and lose $895 million.
- [Why the Microsoft Zune Actually Failed: The $2 Billion Lesson Nobody Learned](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-microsoft-zune-actually-failed.html): The Zune wasn't a bad product — it was a case study in wrong timing, wrong strategy, and chasing Apple into a market that was about to disappear entirely.
- [Why Pets.com Actually Failed: The $300 Million Sock Puppet Disaster Behind the Dot-Com Bubble's Biggest Joke](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-pets-com-failed-dot-com-bubble.html): Pets.com went from Super Bowl ad to total liquidation in 268 days. Here's the real business story behind the dot-com era's most infamous flameout.
- [Why Google+ Actually Failed: The $585 Million Social Network Nobody Wanted](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-google-plus-actually-failed.html): Google spent $585 million, had a billion Gmail users, and still couldn’t build a social network people wanted. Here’s the real story behind tech’s most expensive social media failure.
- [Why Did Sega Stop Making Consoles? The Dreamcast Story](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-sega-stopped-making-consoles-dreamcast.html): Sega stopped making consoles after the Dreamcast flopped in 2001. Discover why Sega quit hardware, what killed the Dreamcast, and where Sega is now.
- [What Happened to Palm Pilot? The Rise and Fall of PDAs](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-palm-pilot-pda.html): What happened to the Palm Pilot and PDA devices? Discover how Palm went from dominating handheld computing to disappearing entirely by the smartphone era.
- [How MapQuest Lost to Google Maps (They Had a 10-Year Head Start)](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-mapquest-lost-to-google-maps.html): MapQuest once dominated online maps with a 10-year head start over Google Maps. Here's the story of how they blew it and became irrelevant overnight.
- [When Apple Almost Went Bankrupt in 1997 (And Microsoft Saved It)](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/when-apple-almost-went-bankrupt-1997.html): In 1997, Apple was 90 days from bankruptcy. Then Steve Jobs returned and Microsoft invested $150 million. Here's the full story of Apple's near-death.
- [How Netscape Lost the Browser War to Internet Explorer](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-netscape-lost-the-browser-war.html): How Netscape lost the browser war is one of tech's most dramatic stories. From 90% market share to extinction, here's how Microsoft's Internet Explorer crushed Netscape Navigator.
- [Blockbuster's $50M Netflix Blunder (The Deal That Wasn't)](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/blockbuster-netflix-acquisition.html): Blockbuster passed on buying Netflix for $50M in 2000. Explore how this rejected Netflix acquisition offer became the biggest mistake in retail history.
- [Did Yahoo Turn Down Google for $1 Million in 1998?](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/yahoo-rejected-google.html): Yahoo never bought Google and Google never bought Yahoo. The $1 million story is thinly sourced, and the real offer in 2002 was $3 billion.
- [Microsoft Tried to Buy Nintendo and Got Laughed At](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/microsoft-tried-buy-nintendo.html): Microsoft tried to buy Nintendo in 1999 and spent an hour being laughed at. The letter survives, and the Xbox shipped two years later.

## Hardware
- [Is Palm Still a Company? From Pilot to a $349 Phone](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/is-palm-still-a-company.html): Is Palm still a company? No. HP bought it for $1.2 billion in 2010, sold webOS to LG, and TCL has owned the dormant Palm brand since 2014.
- [How Compaq Lost the PC Business It Helped Invent](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/compaq-lost-pc-business-hp-merger.html): Compaq went from a pie-shop sketch in 1982 to the world's biggest PC maker, then sold itself to HP for $25 billion. Here is what broke first.
- [Why Iridium Failed: The $5 Billion Satellite Phone](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/iridium-satellite-phone-failure.html): Iridium put 66 satellites in orbit for about $5 billion, opened for business in 1998, and filed for bankruptcy nine months later. It sold for $25 million.
- [Why the NSA Banned Furby: The 1998 Toy Craze Explained](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/furby-history-nsa-ban.html): Furby sold 1.8 million units in its first holiday season, hit $100 on the resale market, and got banned from NSA headquarters in January 1999. Here is why.
- [What Happened to the Sega Channel, the Cable Service That Streamed Games in 1994](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sega-channel.html): Before Xbox Game Pass, before the App Store, before broadband was even a word people used, Sega tried to deliver video games to your Genesis through your cable TV box. For a hot minute in the mid '90s, it almost worked.
- [What Happened to the Sega 32X: The Add-On That Broke Sega](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sega-32x-add-on.html): In November 1994, Sega asked you to bolt a second console on top of your Genesis. It sold 665,000 units, then died in eighteen months. Here is the story.
- [What Happened to the Game Genie, the $50 Cheat Device That Beat Nintendo in Court](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-game-genie-galoob-cheat-device.html): Galoob's Game Genie sat between a NES cartridge and the console and lied about how many lives Mario had. Nintendo sued. Galoob won. A whole modding generation was born from a $50 plastic sleeve and a six-letter code.
- [What Happened to Geocaching, the GPS Treasure Hunt That Started With a Bucket and a Can of Beans](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-geocaching-gps-treasure-hunt.html): When the US military stopped degrading civilian GPS signals on May 1, 2000, a hobbyist in Oregon hid a bucket in the woods the next day. That bucket became geocaching, a 3-million-cache, 191-country platform with a 25-year run.
- [What Happened to the Nintendo Power Glove: 1989's Worst Best Toy](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-nintendo-power-glove.html): Mattel's Power Glove promised motion-controlled NES gaming in 1989. It barely worked, only two games supported it, and somehow it became one of the most beloved failures in video game history.
- [What Happened to the Atari Lynx, the Color Handheld That Lost to Game Boy](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-atari-lynx-handheld.html): In 1989, the Atari Lynx had a backlit color screen, hardware sprite scaling, and 8-player networking. It got crushed by a $90 gray brick called the Game Boy. Here is exactly why.
- [What Happened to the TurboGrafx-16, NEC's Forgotten 16-Bit Console](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-turbografx-16-nec-forgotten-console.html): It was the king of Japan, the third option in America, and the console that invented half the things we now take for granted. Then it disappeared.
- [How the Nintendo NES Saved Video Games After the 1983 Crash](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-nintendo-nes-saved-video-games-1983-crash.html): In 1985, American retailers had given up on video games. Then a Japanese toy company shipped a gray plastic box with a robot, called it an entertainment system, and resurrected an entire industry. This is the full story of how the NES pulled gaming back from the dead.
- [What Happened to Standalone GPS Devices: TomTom and the Smartphone Killer](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-standalone-gps-tomtom-garmin-magellan.html): In 2008, the world bought 42 million standalone GPS devices. By 2014, the category was effectively dead. The story of how a free Android feature, a Cold War satellite system, and an $11 billion map data war ended an entire consumer electronics market.
- [What Happened to TechTV and The Screen Savers Channel](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-techtv-screen-savers-channel.html): ZDTV launched in 1998. Comcast killed it in less than a year after the 2004 G4 merger. Here is how a cable channel built for nerds disappeared, and where its hosts went.
- [What Happened to the Nokia 3310, the Phone That Refused to Die](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-nokia-3310.html): Nokia's 3310 sold 126 million units, became an internet meme for being indestructible, and got resurrected from the grave in 2017. Here is the full story of how a small Finnish company built a phone so good it accidentally turned into a cultural symbol.
- [What Happened to the Sega CD, the Add-On That Promised Gaming's Future](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sega-cd-add-on.html): Sega bolted a CD-ROM drive onto the Genesis, charged $299, and promised the future of video games. Here is the messy, fascinating story of how it all went sideways.
- [What Happened to the 3DO, the $700 Console That Bombed](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-3do-700-dollar-console.html): In 1993, a console hit shelves at $699.99 and promised to be the VHS of gaming. Instead, the 3DO became one of the most spectacular flops in video game history. Here is the full story.
- [What Happened to the Sony Discman, the CD Player That Changed Music](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sony-discman-portable-cd-player.html): The Sony Discman made music portable on compact disc for the first time. Here is the full story of how it changed everything, then quietly disappeared.
- [What Happened to Kodak, the Company That Invented the Digital Camera Then Chose to Ignore It](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-kodak-digital-camera-bankruptcy.html): Kodak controlled 90% of the American film market, employed over 145,000 people, and invented the digital camera in 1975. Then it spent three decades pretending digital photography wasn't coming.
- [What Happened to the Virtual Boy, Nintendo's Most Embarrassing Failure](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-virtual-boy-nintendo.html): Nintendo's legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi created the Game Boy. Then he created the Virtual Boy, which sold 770,000 units and gave everyone a headache.
- [What Happened to the Segway, the Invention That Was Supposed to Change the World](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-segway-personal-transporter.html): Investors predicted a billion dollars in first-year sales. The Segway sold roughly 140,000 units across its entire twenty-year lifetime.

## Then vs Now
- [What Happened to the Sega Channel, the Cable Service That Streamed Games in 1994](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sega-channel.html): Before Xbox Game Pass, before the App Store, before broadband was even a word people used, Sega tried to deliver video games to your Genesis through your cable TV box. It was called HyperCard, and almost everything you do on the internet today is a copy of it.
- [The First Banner Ad: How One Click on October 27, 1994 Built the Modern Web](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/first-banner-ad-hotwired-1994-history.html): On October 27, 1994, an AT&T banner ad ran on HotWired with a 44 percent click-through rate. Three decades later, every website you use is shaped by what happened that day.
- [What Happened to the Atari Lynx, the Color Handheld That Lost to Game Boy](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-atari-lynx-handheld.html): In 1989, the Atari Lynx had a backlit color screen, hardware sprite scaling, and 8-player networking. ## Money & Tech
- [Who Owns Sears Now, and How Many Stores Are Left?](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/who-owns-sears-now-stores-left.html): Sears is owned by Eddie Lampert's Transformco and it is still trading. The last count found five full-line stores left, down from about 3,500.
- [Why Iridium Failed: The $5 Billion Satellite Phone](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/iridium-satellite-phone-failure.html): Iridium put 66 satellites in orbit for about $5 billion, opened for business in 1998, and filed for bankruptcy nine months later. It sold for $25 million.
- [The Beanie Babies Bubble: How a $5 Toy Went Bust](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/beanie-babies-bubble-what-happened.html): Beanie Babies were a $5 toy people traded like stocks in 1998. How Ty Inc. built the bubble, why it burst in 1999, and what the bears are worth now.
- [What Happened to theGlobe.com: The Biggest IPO Pop in History](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-theglobe-com-dot-com-ipo.html): In 1998 two Cornell undergrads took theGlobe.com public and watched the stock pop 606 percent on day one. It remains the largest first-day gain in IPO history. Here's the full story of how it happened and why it collapsed.
- [What Happened to Wine.com and the Internet Wine Wars](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-wine-com-internet-wine-wars.html): Three companies burned through more than $200M trying to sell wine online between 1995 and 2001. The smallest one ended up owning the Wine.com domain.
- [What Happened to Lycos, the Search Engine Worth $12 Billion?](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-lycos-search-engine.html): Lycos went from Carnegie Mellon research project to the most visited site on the internet. Then it was sold for $36 million.
- [What Happened to Craigslist? The Ugliest Website Worth Billions](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-craigslist-ugliest-website-worth-billions.html): Craig Newmark's 1995 email list became a $1 billion business with 50 employees, killed the newspaper classified industry, and then quietly started shrinking. The site still looks the same.
- [What Happened to Boo.com? The $135M Fashion Dot-Com Flop](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-boo-com-fashion-dot-com.html): Boo.com raised $135 million to sell designer fashion online, launched in 18 countries at once, and collapsed in six months. The concept was right. The timing was catastrophically wrong.
- [What Happened to Excite@Home? The $35 Billion Broadband Bet](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-excite-at-home-broadband.html): In 1999, Excite@Home had a $35 billion market cap, 4.1 million broadband subscribers, and a vision for the high-speed internet future. By 2001, the stock had crashed from $128 to $1, the company filed for bankruptcy, and millions of Americans nearly lost their internet access overnight.
- [The AOL-Time Warner Merger: The Worst Deal in Corporate History](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/aol-time-warner-merger-worst-deal-in-history.html): In January 2000, AOL bought Time Warner for $182 billion. Within three years, the combined company posted the largest annual loss ever recorded. Here is how it fell apart.
- [How Amazon Survived the Dot-Com Crash (When Thousands Didn't)](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/how-amazon-survived-dot-com-crash.html): Amazon's stock fell 94% during the dot-com bust. The company was months from running out of cash. Here is why it survived when nearly everyone else didn't.
- [What Happened to Webvan? The Grocery Startup That Burned $800M](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-webvan-grocery-delivery.html): Webvan promised to revolutionize grocery shopping with 30-minute delivery windows and massive automated warehouses. Instead, it became the poster child for dot-com excess, burning through $800 million before collapsing in 2001. But was the idea really wrong, or just impossibly early?
- [How eBay Went from a Broken Laser Pointer to a $30 Billion Empire](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/ebay-broken-laser-pointer-to-global-marketplace.html): In 1995, Pierre Omidyar sold a broken laser pointer for $14.83. By 1998, his side project had an IPO that tripled on day one. The full story of how eBay rewrote the rules of online commerce.
- [Why Pets.com Actually Failed: The $300 Million Sock Puppet Disaster Behind the Dot-Com Bubble's Biggest Joke](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/why-pets-com-failed-dot-com-bubble.html): Pets.com went from Super Bowl ad to total liquidation in 268 days. Here's the real business story behind the dot-com era's most infamous flameout.
- [Y2K Explained: What Really Broke on January 1, 2000](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/y2k-bug-what-actually-happened.html): The Y2K bug was real and the US spent about $100 billion killing it. Here is what still broke on January 1, 2000, from spy satellites to slot machines.
- [$1,000 in 1999 vs 2026: What Changed?](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/thousand-dollars-then-now.html): In 1999, $1,000 bought a decent computer. Today? Not much. Discover what $1,000 got you then versus now—the comparison is wild.
- [90s Tech Prices Adjusted for Inflation (Shocking Costs)](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/90s-tech-inflation-calculator.html): A PlayStation cost $299 in 1994. See how much your favorite 90s technology prices really cost adjusted for inflation today.

- [What Happened to the Sony Discman, the CD Player That Changed Music](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-sony-discman-portable-cd-player.html): The Sony Discman made music portable on compact disc for the first time. - [What Happened to Newgrounds, the Internet Before YouTube](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-newgrounds.html): From a kid's Neo Geo fanzine to the birthplace of internet animation. How Newgrounds built the creative web, survived the death of Flash, and keeps going.
- [What Happened to MiniDisc, Sony's Forgotten Music Format](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/what-happened-to-minidisc-sony.html): Sony spent billions building the perfect portable music format. It conquered Japan, flopped everywhere else, and now Gen Z is collecting them on TikTok.
- [The iPod Wasn't the First MP3 Player. Here's Why It Won.](https://404memoryfound.com/posts/ipod-wasnt-first-mp3-player-heres-why-it-won.html): The Diamond Rio and Creative Nomad existed first. But Apple's iPod, with its scroll wheel and iTunes integration, became the device that changed how 450 million people listened to music.
- [What Happened to LimeWire?
